clue.text: Cockney listens - and bows (4)

indicators.note: A Cockney accent drops the aitch off the front of a word, and it is the spoken version, not the written one, that the clue hands you.

blocks.note: To hark is to listen — 'hark at him', 'hark the herald angels'.
With the aitch gone, what is left is said aloud and comes out spelt a different way.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bows' first reads as the ones you tie, or the ones you take on stage. The archer's is the one meant, and it is the shape of it that matters.
explanation.definitionFit: An archer's bow is a curve, so 'bows' names curved lines — the geometric sense of the word, not the knot or the stage exit.

clue.text: Silly Carol, happy to be uncertain (10)

indicators.note: Silly here means scatterbrained rather than merely foolish, and a scatterbrained arrangement is one that has lost the order it was given in.

blocks.note: A woman's name and the adjective after it supply all ten letters between them.

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman's fodder is often a first name plus an adjective, and the step that costs solvers time is seeing that Carol is wanted for her letters, not as a person.
explanation.definitionFit: An apocryphal story is one of doubtful authenticity, endlessly repeated but never verified, so 'uncertain' names that unreliable standing.

clue.text: Tricky situation: farm with no cows to flounder (3,2,5)

indicators.note: To flounder is to thrash about without getting anywhere, and letters thrashing about end up somewhere other than where they started.

blocks.note: 'with' only joins them: farm, no and cows between them supply the ten letters.

explanation.walkthrough: A farm with no cows sounds like a subtraction, and it is not: nothing is taken away. All three words stay and hand over every letter they have.
explanation.definitionFit: Opening a can of worms means starting something that turns messy and cannot be tidied away again, which is the tricky situation meant.

clue.text: Reproduces dodgy systems (10)

indicators.note: Something dodgy cannot be trusted to stay as it looks, so the word warns you the letters beside it will not stay where they are.

blocks.note: The opening word is the raw material, and its ten letters match the enumeration exactly.

explanation.walkthrough: A three-word clue leaves nowhere to hide, and the trap is taking the first word as the definition. Count its letters against the enumeration and it is plainly the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Procedures are the settled ways an organisation does things, and a system is likewise a fixed method — the plurals line up step for step.

clue.text: Decrees - when you've repeatedly drawn a line? (7)

definitions.text: when you've repeatedly drawn a line

blocks.note: The legal sense: what a judge or a referee formally hands down.

blocks.clueFragment: when you've repeatedly drawn a line
blocks.note: The other sense of the verb: to rule is to draw a line against a straight edge, and doing it more than once makes it plural.

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter owning up to the second reading. One word covers a courtroom and a pencil case, and only the plural joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: Rulings are the decisions a judge or referee hands down, which is what decrees are; the second sense takes the verb back to the ruler that draws lines.

clue.text: Some welcome Dickensian characters being amusing (7)

indicators.note: Some of a phrase is a part of it and not the whole, which is the signal that a run of what follows is to be lifted out untouched.
Characters are letters as well as people in a novel, and it is the letters of the words before it that are wanted.

blocks.note: Seven consecutive letters run from the middle of the first word straight on into the second, needing no rearrangement.

explanation.walkthrough: Dickens wrote characters, so the surface gives nothing away — which is exactly what a hidden word needs. The join between the two words is where to look.
explanation.definitionFit: Comedic means belonging to comedy, so a comedic turn is a funny one, and 'amusing' is the everyday adjective for that same quality.

clue.text: Twin to put lid on some whisky (6,6)

blocks.note: A twin is a double — one of an identical pair.
To scotch a rumour is to put a lid on it and stop it dead.

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is doing two jobs at once: the verb that kills a rumour builds the word, while the drink is what the finished phrase orders at a bar.
explanation.definitionFit: A double Scotch is two measures of Scotch whisky in one glass, so 'some whisky' names the drink by the amount poured.

clue.text: Most of logbook picked up in police swoop (4)

indicators.note: Most of a word is nearly all of it, which in practice means every letter but the last one.
Picked up means lifted, and a down entry read from the bottom upwards delivers its letters in the opposite order.

blocks.note: A logbook is filled in day by day, which is what a diary is for.
Take all but the final letter of those five and four are left to turn round.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' reads as gossip overheard, which is how it slips past as an instruction — and in a down clue it can only mean read the letters upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A raid is a sudden descent by police on premises, so 'police swoop' is the newspaper phrase for exactly that operation.

clue.text: Notice function making noise (4)

indicators.note: Making noise is saying the thing out loud, so what counts is how the word sounds and not how it is spelt.

blocks.note: The trigonometric function that sits beside cosine and tangent; said aloud it is written another way entirely.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Function' looks like it wants to be a party or a job, and it is neither — it is the one from school trigonometry, and only its sound is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A sign is a notice put up to be read: the placard sense of the word, not the verb meaning to spot something.

clue.text: Sound from pen - why pen no use? (4)

blocks.note: The riddle framing: a pen is no use when it has nothing in it. Its two pieces are taken below.
Nothing is written as a round zero, which doubles as the letter.
The second one is the writing kind, and what it runs on is ink.

explanation.walkthrough: Two different pens sit in this clue: the first is a sty, the second writes. Everyman reuses the word on purpose, so it belongs to the definition and to the wordplay both.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen is also a pig's enclosure, so the sound coming out of one is a grunt, and the answer is the comic-strip spelling of that grunt.

clue.text: Clutch, clutching loved one, making racket (10)

indicators.note: To clutch something is to close your hand right round it, so whatever is clutched ends up inside the word doing the clutching.

blocks.note: To clutch at a rail is to cling to it.
Amour is the French for love and is used in English for a lover — 'a secret amour'.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Clutch' and 'clutching' sit side by side doing different jobs: the first is the word to be opened up, the second is the instruction to open it.
explanation.definitionFit: To clamour is to shout insistently and all at once, which is making a racket — the noisy sense rather than the 'clamouring for reform' one.

clue.text: What guard's doing: not selling retirement gift? (7,5)

blocks.note: If you are not selling something, you are keeping it.
The traditional present for a long-serving employee on retirement is a gold watch.

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by tradition rather than by dictionary: not every leaver gets one, but every crossword leaver does.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep watch is to stay alert and look out for trouble, which is a sentry's whole job, so the -ing form matches what a guard is doing.

clue.text: Playing Lendl: a four-time French tennis ace (6,5)

indicators.note: To play with something is to move it about idly, and what is being moved about here is the letters that follow, not a racket.

blocks.note: Ivan Lendl, eight times a grand slam champion, is wanted only for his five letters.
The letter A, taken four times over, exactly as the words say.
Fr. is the usual abbreviation for French, the one a dictionary uses to label a borrowed word.

explanation.walkthrough: The hard step is reading 'a four-time' literally. It is not describing a champion; it is asking for one letter written out four times over.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Tennis ace' defines by example: an ace is a top player, and the Spaniard who owns the French Open clay-court record is one.

clue.text: Assignments making reformed crooks howl (10)

definitions.note: The answer is a mass noun — you never speak of two of them — so the plural 'Assignments' names the several separate tasks that one uncountable word covers.

indicators.note: Reformed is re-formed, made into a new shape, and a word re-formed is one whose letters have been put together differently.

blocks.note: The two words after the indicator give up all ten of their letters.

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a police story — reformed criminals, howling — and it hangs together so well that the ten letters sitting in plain sight take a while to notice.
explanation.definitionFit: Schoolwork is the set of tasks a pupil is given to get through, in class or at home, which is what a teacher calls assignments.

clue.text: Chimney-cleaners draw in drawing of lots (10)

blocks.note: A chimney sweep cleans the flue; put in the plural the job title gives six letters.
A stall that draws in a hundred pounds a day takes a hundred pounds a day.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw' appears twice and means two different things: money coming in for the wordplay, and a name pulled out of a hat for the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweepstake is a lottery in which the whole pot goes to whoever's name comes out, so 'drawing of lots' describes how the winner is picked.

clue.text: Spurs very quietly storm off ... (7)

indicators.note: Milk that has gone off has turned, and a word told to go off turns the same way — its letters no longer in the state they were handed over in.

blocks.note: Pianissimo, the score's marking for very quiet, is written as a doubled p.
The five letters of the word itself join the two above.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spurs' opens the clue looking like Tottenham Hotspur, the London football club, and 'storm off' looks like what a beaten team does. Both readings belong to the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To prompt someone is to spur them into speech or action, which is the theatre sense too: the prompt feeds an actor the line they have lost.

clue.text: ... decrepit coach, exhausted, wants steady source of income (4,3)

indicators.note: Something decrepit has fallen apart with age, and letters that have fallen apart no longer sit in the order they were given in.
A thing exhausted has had everything inside it used up, so what survives is only what sits at either end.

blocks.note: The five letters of the word itself, before they are shaken up.
Empty the middle out of the second word and its first and last letters are what remain.

explanation.walkthrough: The commas are load-bearing. 'Exhausted' looks like it describes the coach, and the sentence reads perfectly that way — but the word it hollows is the one after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A cash cow is a product that keeps earning with little effort, milked like a dairy herd, so it is a steady source of income rather than a windfall.

clue.text: Beggar me! Niagara's surrounding country (7)

indicators.note: What surrounds a thing sits on both sides of it, so the words named are the wrapping and what is wanted lies inside them.

blocks.note: Seven letters run on without a break from the end of the first word, through the second and into the third; the punctuation is ignored.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Beggar me!' is an old exclamation of astonishment, thrown in purely to smuggle its last two letters into the run. Hidden words often begin mid-word like this.
explanation.definitionFit: Armenia is a landlocked country in the Caucasus, south of Georgia, so 'country' names it by the class it belongs to.

clue.text: Bling: grotesque slanket (7)

definitions.note: Bling is an uncountable word for flashy jewellery, so it names the category rather than agreeing in number with the plural answer.

indicators.note: A grotesque figure is one distorted out of its proper shape, and a word distorted out of its proper shape has its letters somewhere new.

blocks.note: A slanket is a blanket with sleeves, sold as loungewear; here it is simply seven letters.

explanation.walkthrough: A colon after a one-word definition is Everyman's favourite joinery, and everything on the far side of it is indicator plus fodder and nothing else.
explanation.definitionFit: Anklets are ornamental chains worn round the ankle, and bling is the slang term for showy jewellery of exactly that kind.

clue.text: In favour of 'very average'!? Everyman's beginning to annoy (7)

indicators.note: The beginning of a word is where it starts, so what is taken from it is the single letter it starts with.

blocks.note: Pro means in favour of — pro-reform, the pros and cons.
v. is the everyday abbreviation for very, as in 'v. good'.
Something merely OK is average: neither good nor bad.
Everyman is this setter's own pen name, and what it begins with is its first letter.

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman signs his clues, so his name inside one is nearly always letters rather than a person. The quotation marks are the hint that 'very average' is two pieces, not one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To provoke someone is to needle them until they react, so 'annoy' is the milder everyday synonym for the same deliberate act.

clue.text: Initially powerful realm; ultimately subservient state ignobly abolished! (7)

definitions.text: Initially powerful realm; ultimately subservient state ignobly abolished!

indicators.note: Initially means at the very start, and set in front of a run of words it asks for the letter each of them starts with.

blocks.note: The first three words of the run hand over the letters they begin with, semicolon and all.
The last four do the same, and the letters arrive in the order the clue reads.

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here is left over for a definition, because the sentence is the definition: seven words of history, each one also giving up its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Every word reads straight as history — the realm rose, was reduced to a rubber stamp under the Nazis, and was dissolved by Allied decree in 1947.

clue.text: Warnings as Spooner relays outcome of birthday-party food fight (4-2,5)

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner was famous for trading the opening sounds of two words, so having him relay a phrase means it arrives with those sounds swapped.

blocks.note: The food at the centre of a birthday party is the cake, and a fight ends with it up the walls.
Say that aloud with the opening sounds of the outer words traded, C for W.

explanation.walkthrough: A spoonerism always names its speaker, so the clue tells you which two sounds to swap before you have any idea what you are swapping them in.
explanation.definitionFit: A wake-up call is the jolt that makes somebody face a problem, so 'Warnings' is the figurative sense — the hotel's morning telephone call turned metaphor.

clue.text: Mucky film showing Special Constable with hesitant expression (4)

blocks.note: A special constable is a volunteer part-time police officer in Britain, and SC is the rank's short form.
The noise you make out loud while you hunt for the next word.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mucky film' sets up a seedy movie, and the answer turns out to be nothing so interesting: it is the layer that forms on top of standing water.
explanation.definitionFit: Scum is the dirty layer that gathers on the surface of a liquid, so 'film' is meant in its thin-coating sense, not its cinema one.

clue.text: Decent trade show (4)

blocks.note: The sense of adequate rather than admirable: a decent effort, a middling grade.
The industry gathering where firms take a stand and show off what they sell.

explanation.walkthrough: Three words and no wordplay, so the whole trick is the join: 'Decent trade' reads as one phrase, which is what stops you splitting the clue in the right place.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair means decent in the sense of acceptable rather than excellent, and a trade fair is the exhibition where an industry shows off its wares.

clue.text: Once again, apply following diagram depicting something intoxicating (10)

indicators.note: To follow is to come after, so the piece it governs is set down behind the other rather than in front of it.

blocks.note: A chart is a diagram of figures — a bar chart, a flow chart.
To apply something once again is to put it to use a second time.

explanation.walkthrough: Chartreuse is a fiercely strong herbal liqueur made by Carthusian monks in the French Alps, and the yellow-green colour is named after the drink rather than the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: The liqueur is about 55% alcohol, so 'something intoxicating' points at the drink and not at the colour that borrowed its name.

clue.text: End-piece: a physician taken aback (4)

indicators.note: To be taken aback is to be pushed backwards, and in an across entry backwards means reading the letters right to left.

blocks.note: Doc is the familiar short form for a doctor, with the article kept in front of it.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken aback' reads as the doctor being startled, which is exactly what a good reversal indicator does: it describes a person while instructing the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A coda is the passage that rounds off a piece of music, so 'End-piece' names it by where it sits rather than by what it contains.

clue.text: It says you'll go wrong adding potato to cabbage salad (7,3)

blocks.note: Murphy is an old informal British word for a potato, borrowed from the Irish surname.
Slaw, as in coleslaw, is shredded cabbage dressed as a salad.

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is invisible in the wordplay: the two chunks run straight together and it is the solver who puts the punctuation back in.
explanation.definitionFit: The law is the maxim that anything which can go wrong will go wrong, so the definition simply states what the named principle asserts.

clue.text: Island on vacation - Sark - yippee! (4)

indicators.note: A house on vacation stands empty, and a word emptied the same way keeps only the letters at each end.

blocks.note: Sark is one of the Channel Islands; emptied out, its first and last letters are left.
The shout of delight, hollowed the same way, leaves the letters at its ends.

explanation.walkthrough: One indicator serving two words is the economy that makes a four-letter clue work, and the surface — an island, a holiday, a cheer — never lets on.
explanation.definitionFit: Skye is the largest of the Inner Hebrides, off the west coast of Scotland, so 'Island' names it by the category it belongs to.
